clues.title: Plate: white, mix of short and long
text: The standard licence plates are white and can be **short or long**. In street view, you will often see a mix of both sizes.

Commercial vehicles, such as taxis or buses, can have older [solid orange](https://goo.gl/maps/QHw5nYaBYjsWqeNo7) plates, or newer ones with an [orange bar](https://goo.gl/maps/F5SCJqkGQ7QFR9kb7) at the top.
NOTE: Ecuador is the only country in Latin America to use a mix of short and long licence plates.

images.caption: Ecuadorian plates: standard short, standard long, new and old commercial

clues.summary: Standard plates are white and come in both short and long sizes, often mixed together. Taxis and buses have orange plates or an orange bar on top. No other Latin American country mixes sizes.

clues.title: Google car: white car, short stubby antenna
text: All Generation 3 coverage is made with a white car, with a **short and thick antenna **(“stubby antenna”). The antenna and or car are not always visible.
NOTE: Mexico, Brazil and Colombia can also have this same short antenna.
This antenna on a black car can only be found in Colombia, which can help with tough 50-50s with Ecuador. Note that Colombia can also simply have a white car.
clues.summary: The older Gen 3 car is white with a short, thick antenna, though car or antenna may be hidden. Mexico, Brazil and Colombia can show the same antenna.

clues.title: Google car: white pickup, black trunk
text: All Generation 4 coverage was captured using a** white pickup truck** with a **black trunk** and** no antenna**.
NOTE: The pickup truck in Panama and Costa Rica has an antenna on the front.
clues.summary: The newer Gen 4 car is a white pickup truck with a black cover on the bed and no antenna. Panama and Costa Rica pickups have an antenna at the front.

differs.how: Pickup has an antenna on the front
Pickup has an antenna on the front

clues.title: Camera: low-quality Ari with wide blur
text: Google used a weird, low-quality camera in Ecuador. This camera is known as the official Ari (or “Shitcam”). It has a wide circular car blur and often somewhat brownish colours. You will sometimes see a unique [red logo](https://maps.app.goo.gl/iWqtJ8ZuSgxFhEJ8A) at the front of the car.
NOTE: Within Latin America, Ecuador is the only country that has shitcam coverage.

images.caption: Mountain road; the inset circle at top right is labelled 'sometimes visible' and shows part of the camera

clues.summary: A low-quality camera with a wide round car blur and brownish colours. You sometimes see a red logo at the front. No other Latin American country has this camera.

clues.title: Bollard: round red stripes or flat black panel
text: Ecuador is one of the few Latin American countries where bollards are very common.
You will find two main types of bollards:
- A **round** bollard with two red stripes,
- A **flat** bollard with two red reflectors on black.
Many other bollards can be found, however, they will almost always have the same colour scheme and style.
NOTE: A similar rectangular bollard can sometimes be found in Malaysia.
clues.summary: Bollards are very common here. One is round with two red stripes, the other flat with two red reflectors on black. Malaysia can have a similar flat one.

differs.how: Sometimes has a similar rectangular bollard

clues.title: Pole: concrete with ladder-like indents
text: Most poles in Ecuador are [round](https://goo.gl/maps/8mA5mVbq65jxoxuB9) and made of concrete. These poles are fairly generic and not all that useful to identify the country.

However, sometimes you will see another, more useful type of concrete pole: the **ladder pole**. It has a lot of small indents – resembling the steps of a ladder. Within Latin America, these poles are more or less unique to Ecuador.
NOTE: Brazilian waffle poles also have indents, but only a couple – as opposed to the large amount of indents that Ecuadorian ladder poles have.

images.caption: Red circles compare a round pole (left) with a ladder pole (right)

clues.summary: Most poles are plain round concrete, not very helpful. The useful one is the ladder pole, with many small indents like rungs. Brazil's waffle poles have far fewer indents.

differs.how: Waffle poles have only a couple of indents

clues.title: Road: concrete road surface
text: **Concrete roads** are relatively common in Ecuador.
clues.summary: Roads made of concrete slabs are fairly common.

clues.title: Guardrail: double guardrails
text: **Double guardrails** are very commonly used. This is much less common in other South American countries.
clues.summary: Roads often have two stacked metal guardrails. This is much less common in other South American countries.

clues.title: Chevron: many chevrons in each curve
text: Ecuador often uses a lot of chevrons in road curves (“**chevron spam**”), usually considerably more than most other Latin American countries.
NOTE: Colombia also occasionally uses a lot of chevrons in curves.
clues.summary: Curves have far more chevron signs than in most Latin American countries. Colombia also sometimes uses many.

clues.title: Sign: square white road signs
text: Ecuador uses a lot of **square road signs** with a white background, of the design shown in the image.
clues.summary: Many road signs are square with a white background, in the design shown in the image.

clues.title: Kilometre marker: green with highway shield
text: Kilometre markers are green and have the distinctive Ecuadorian **highway shields** on them.
clues.summary: Green kilometre markers carry the national highway shield.

clues.title: Sign back: teal blue paint
text: Sometimes, the back of the signs are painted a **teal blue** colour. The signposts are thin and made of metal.
NOTE: Ecuador is the only country in Latin America to use teal blue sign backs.

images.caption: Red circle marks the teal-blue painted back of a road sign, left

clues.summary: The back of signs is sometimes painted teal blue, on thin metal posts. No other Latin American country does this.

clues.title: Sign: one-way and two-way arrows
text: Ecuador uses these signs to indicate one or two-way streets.

NOTE: The [Dominican Republic](https://maps.app.goo.gl/NbmAmmV68vqXA6JW9) and [Puerto Rico](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7ihNZDn6wtVLZ1187) are the only two other Latin American countries to use similar signs with **text inside the arrow**.
clues.summary: Street direction signs have the text written inside an arrow. In Latin America only the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico use similar signs.

clues.title: Houses: grey bricks and metal roofs
text: Most houses are made of grey bricks and have metal roofs.
NOTE: This is not unique to Ecuador, but is very common. Countries such as Peru, and especially Bolivia, commonly use red bricks.
clues.summary: Most houses are grey brick with metal roofs. This is common but not unique. Peru and especially Bolivia use more red bricks.

clues.title: Pavement: hexagonal tiles
text: In urban areas, you can sometimes find this pavement consisting of **hexagonal tiles**.

images.caption: Hexagonal paving tiles on a street; the red circle zooms in on the tile shape

clues.summary: In towns you sometimes see pavement made of hexagon-shaped tiles.

clues.title: Coverage: mostly the west, gaps in the Amazon
text: Most of the coverage in Ecuador is centred around the **western part** of the country. A large part of the Amazon rainforest has no coverage.
There is also some trekker coverage on the Galapagos Islands.
You can check out the extent of the official coverage [on this website](https://sv-map.netlify.app#base=roadmap&cov=official&zoom=7&center=-1.7300837111164604%2C-77.11303710937501).
clues.summary: Most coverage is in the western part. Much of the Amazon has none. The Galapagos Islands have some backpack coverage.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 4 across most of the country
text: Generation 4 coverage is found in most of Ecuador, with notable gaps in the northwest and southeast.
clues.summary: The newer Gen 4 coverage is found in most of the country, with gaps in the northwest and southeast.

clues.title: Google car: high or low antenna wire
text: The Google car antenna has two distinct variations:
- The “**high**” antenna (purple), where the wire around the antenna is entirely above the halfway line of the antenna.
- And the “**low**” antenna (blue) where the majority of the wire is below the halfway point of the line, and there can be a small bit poking up at the very top.
This is most useful when you have the high antenna, since it will always be in the northern half of the country.

images.caption: Two close-ups of the antenna wire outlined in blue, one high and one low

clues.summary: The antenna comes in two types. On the high one, the wire is all above the halfway line. On the low one, most wire is below it. A high antenna always means the northern half.

clues.title: Landscape: Andes in the middle
text: This is an **elevation map** of Ecuador. The imposing Andes mountains run through the middle of the country. The east and west of the country are more flat.
clues.summary: The Andes mountains run through the middle of the country, while the east and the west are flatter.

clues.title: Plants: banana plantations
text: **Banana plants**, and especially plantations, are most commonly found in the southwestern part of the country.
clues.summary: Banana plants and big plantations are mostly found in the southwest.

clues.title: Landscape: very dry coast
text: This extremely **dry landscape** is only found in the coastal region between Guayaquil and Manta.
clues.summary: A very dry, bare landscape found only on the coast between Guayaquil and Manta.

clues.title: Landscape: very flat land
text: The **flattest** region is located around the city of Guayaquil. This is most easily seen on the [E-25](https://www.google.com/maps/@-2.3393014,-79.635075,3a,90y,317.73h,97.87t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s7gNj0DBNsq092c8zyxNlsg!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) and [E-48](https://www.google.com/maps/@-1.6742465,-79.9878759,3a,90y,224.78h,88.98t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sFvgH8Prb3g9q16A6jg0ecw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu). The Amazon area is also very flat, and will be described below.
clues.summary: The flattest area is around the big southwestern port city, easiest to see on the E-25 and E-48 roads. The Amazon area is flat too.

clues.title: Vegetation: white-barked trees and oil palms
text: The **Amazon** area is very distinct. It is fairly flat, and contains many of these trees with white bark (Cordia trichotoma), and oil palms.
The vast majority of the coverage notably uses the rarer “high antenna”.
clues.summary: A flat area with many white-barked trees and oil palms is the Amazon. Almost all of its coverage uses the rarer high antenna.

clues.title: Landscape: Amazon look but hilly
text: The province of **Esmeraldas** can look similar to the Amazon region, but it is significantly hillier.
clues.summary: A rainforest look similar to the Amazon, but much hillier, points to the northwest coast province of Esmeraldas.

clues.title: Landscape: winding mountain roads
text: The southern regions have many winding **mountain roads** and exposed brownish **red dirt**.
The central provinces can have similar roads, but the exposed dirt will usually not be found in these areas.
clues.summary: In the south, mountain roads wind through exposed reddish-brown soil. The central provinces have similar roads, but usually without the bare dirt.

clues.title: Vegetation: dry land with many pines
text: The province of Chimborazo is semi-arid, and has an abundance of **pine trees**.
clues.summary: A semi-dry area with lots of pine trees points to the province of Chimborazo in the central mountains.

clues.title: Plate: taxi first letter shows the province
text: Taxis in Ecuador are very common, and the **first letter** on each taxi can be used to determine the province you are in. The first letter of the taxi and the first letter of the province name are often the same.

NOTE: This letter will also appear as the first letter on ordinary licence plates respectively in each region. Beware that the letter P, as the letter for Pichincha (the region containing Quito), shows up occasionally in several regions.

images.caption: Taxi with its province letter painted on the roof, circled with an arrow

clues.summary: Taxis are common, and the first letter on the plate usually matches the province name's first letter. The same letter starts normal plates. P, for the Quito area, shows up in many regions.

clues.title: Pole: concrete with oval see-through holes
text: Electricity poles with **oval, see-through holes** are most common in Loja province. They are occasionally found in neighbouring provinces.
clues.summary: Electricity poles with oval holes through them are most common in the southern province of Loja, and sometimes found in neighbouring provinces.

clues.title: Guardrail: black and yellow painted
text: Guardrails in Guayas province are often painted **black-and-yellow**, as opposed to the generic silver or solid yellow versions.
clues.summary: Guardrails painted black and yellow, instead of plain silver or solid yellow, point to the province around the big southwestern port city, Guayas.

clues.title: Road: divided highway in dry coast area
text: The E-40 between Salinas and Guayaquil is one of the only **divided highways** in Ecuador, and the only one in the **dry area** near the southwestern coast.
clues.summary: A divided highway (the E-40 between Salinas and Guayaquil) is one of the few in the country, and the only one in the dry southwest coast.

clues.title: Roadside: brown pipe along the road
text: A brown pipe can be seen on the side of a few north-eastern Ecuadorian roads.
clues.summary: A brown pipe runs alongside a few roads in the north-east.

clues.title: Coverage: islands with backpack and boat only
text: [The Galapagos Islands](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Gal%C3%A1pagos+Islands/@-0.383106,-90.4233344,8z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x9021d9b43bec07cd:0xfb3e68fef05dae23!8m2!3d-0.383106!4d-90.4233344!16zL20vMDE2empq?entry=ttu) are an archipelago located west of mainland Ecuador. There are only **trekkers** and **boat coverage** on and around the islands. There is a wide variety of landscapes, including volcanic soil, low shrubbery, and craters (with Galapagos turtles onlooking).
clues.summary: The Galapagos Islands, west of the mainland, only have backpack and boat coverage. Landscapes range from volcanic soil and low shrubs to craters, sometimes with giant tortoises.

clues.title: Camera: low-quality Ari in South America
text: If you have vibes that you are in South America and coverage was taken using "shitcam" camera you gonna be in Ecuador. There is "shitcam" in other countries but in South America you can only find "shitcam" in Ecuador.
Note: Ecuador also has GEN3(and little bit of GEN4) coverage not only shitcam! So don't discard Ecuador if it's not shitcam.

images.caption: Low-resolution Ari camera view with a wide circular blur only at the bottom, labelled as a poor camera

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: If you see this low-quality camera in South America, it is Ecuador, which is the only country there with it. Ecuador also has Gen 3 and some Gen 4, so don't rule it out when the camera looks normal.

clues.title: Road: grey, dirty coastal road with a beach
text: One road on the southern east coast of Ecuador looks a lot like a gray, dirty, depressing version of Tumbes or Piura, just with more garbage. It has an offshoot with a pretty beach.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: One road on the southern east coast looks like a grey, dirty version of the nearby northern Peru coast, with more garbage. A side road leads to a pretty beach.
